PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 1

Alphabet & Letter Sounds

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 1Subjects Letters, sounds & matching

Twenty-six alphabet cards, a whole pile of familiar things to name, and printable sheets to solve at the table. This is the first preschool class on the path — built for three-year-old pacing, which means short, playful and always allowed to stop.

You do not need to teach the whole alphabet today. Start with a few letters that catch your child’s eye — the first letter of their name is the classic winner — and let the rest wait for next time.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, little one on the lap or roaming — both work.

TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Five little steps, in any order that suits you: a welcome from your teacher, the letter cards, big-and-little letters on the printed sheets, an off-screen hunt, and a warm goodbye. Stop after any step — that is a complete class, and there is never a score at the end.

  1. 1 Teacher welcome
  2. 2 Learn the letters
  3. 3 Solve the sheets
  4. 4 Take it off screen
  5. 5 Class complete

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the alphabet sheets together.

The twenty-six letter cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and named, they are the class’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twenty-six, two to a page. Cut them out together, saying each letter’s name as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Say letter, then sound

    Hold up a card and say both in one breath — “B, and it says buh”. Then let your child have the card and take a turn.

  3. 03

    Sort big and little

    Lay the cards out and find each big letter’s little partner. Same letter, different size — matching them is real letter work.

  4. 04

    Trace, then color

    Pick today’s card and trace its big letter with one finger, then a crayon. On screen, the card page has a Write & Color layer that does the same job.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Letters that live in your house.

The alphabet sticks best away from the screen, in short playful moments. Pick one of these — two minutes is plenty — and follow your child’s lead.

Find their own letter

  • Say the first letter of your child’s name and look for it on cups, clothes and cereal boxes.
  • “That’s your letter!” is the whole game — and it never gets old.

Letter hunt on a book cover

  • Hold up a favourite picture book and ask, “Can you find a letter you know on the cover?”
  • Any letter they spot is a win — name it warmly and move on.

Playdough letters

  • Roll a long rope of playdough and bend it into the first letter of your child’s name — or today’s favourite card letter.
  • Letters you can squeeze are letters you remember.

Letters out in the world

  • On a walk or a shop trip, point out letters on signs and packaging — “Look, an S like sun!”
  • Keep it light: one or two letters per outing is exactly right.

Stay close, keep it playful and stop while it is still fun. There is nothing to finish here.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

At three, letter play is recognition play: naming, noticing and drawing — not drilling or handwriting. If your child mixes up b and d, or loves Q only for its tail, that is exactly on track. The printed sheets and the Write & Color layer keep every sound claim on the cards honest — including x, which mostly ends words rather than starting them.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Sit together for the card viewing — laps are the best seats in the house. Name the letter and say its sound in the same breath — “B, and it says buh” — then move on quickly. Letter names and letter sounds are both worth knowing, and mixing them in play keeps either one from feeling like a test.

On the printed sheets, let the finger do the tracing first and the crayon second. On screen, let your child do the drawing in the Write & Color layer — even when the letter looks wobbly; the finger teaches the eye.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class is two letters traced on a printed sheet, today’s class was a success.

    Letter A — Apple.

    Big A, little a and a shiny red apple — the friendliest place to start the alphabet, because snack time has already done half of the teaching.

    THE CARD — DRAW RIGHT ON IT

    Trace A a, circle the apple.

    This is A’s own card from the class. Pick a crayon, then trace the big letter and the little letter right on the card with your finger, a stylus or the mouse — and circle apple. Press Save my work when you are proud: your drawing stays here for next time.

    THE LETTER SOUND

    What does A say?

    “a — aaa, like the very start of apple”

    The letter is named A, but in apple you hear its sound: aaa — the first sound out of your mouth. A is a vowel with more than one sound; this short a is the friendliest one to start with.

    TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

    Apple taste test.

    Two minutes is plenty. Follow your child’s lead and stop while it is still fun — that is the whole method.

    1. 01

      Cut three fruits into slices — an apple and two others.

    2. 02

      Say aaa each time your child tastes the apple: aaa, apple!

    3. 03

      Ask which of the three fruits starts with aaa, and let your child be the judge.

    “c — kuh, like cat”

    Letter D — Dog.

    A happy orange dog with its tail up, for the letter D. If your family has a dog, this card will be requested every single day.

    THE CARD — DRAW RIGHT ON IT

    Trace D d, circle the dog.

    THE LETTER SOUND

    What does D say?

    “d — duh, like dog”

    D says duh, a quick tongue tap behind the teeth, like the start of dog. Say it fast — duh — and never duh-uh; the short version is the one that helps with reading.

    2. 02

      Teach your dog a trick — roll over, sit, stay — saying duh with each command.

    3. 03

      Finish with a big dog shake and a laugh.

    Letter F — Fish.

    The letters F f swim in with a teal fish. F is a windy, whispery letter — you can feel it on your lip, which makes it irresistible to children.

    THE LETTER SOUND

    What does F say?

    “f — fff, a long windy sound”

    F says fff — a long, windy sound made with top teeth on the bottom lip. Hold it out: fffff. If it tickles your lip, you are doing it right.

    2. 02

      Blow a tissue up in the air with a long fffff and catch it.

    3. 03

      Finish with five fast fish kisses — pop your lips like a fish five times.

    Letter G — Giraffe.

    The letters G g arrive beside a yellow giraffe — the letter with two voices, and the animal that proves the alphabet is full of surprises.

    THE CARD — DRAW RIGHT ON IT

    Trace G g, circle the giraffe.

    This is G’s own card from the class. Pick a crayon, then trace the big letter and the little letter right on the card with your finger, a stylus or the mouse — and circle giraffe. Press Save my work when you are proud: your drawing stays here for next time.

    THE LETTER SOUND

    What does G say?

    “g — in giraffe it says j”

    G has two sounds, and our giraffe teaches the tricky one: in giraffe, g says j. In goat, game and go it says the harder g. Both are right — giraffe simply picked the j sound.

    G keeps a second sound, the hard g in goat and game. Giraffe picked the j sound — both are correct.

    TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

    Giraffe stretch.

    Two minutes is plenty. Follow your child’s lead and stop while it is still fun — that is the whole method.

    1. 01

      Reach up high like a giraffe reaching leaves: j, j, giraffe!

    2. 02

      Munch imaginary leaves with slow, chewing bites.

    3. 03

      Walk with long stiff legs back to the sofa and rest your long neck.

    Letter I — Ice Cream.

    The letter I melts in with an ice cream cone. I is the only letter that introduces itself by name here — ice starts with ie, just like the letter’s own name.

    THE CARD — DRAW RIGHT ON IT

    Trace I i, circle the ice cream.

    This is I’s own card from the class. Pick a crayon, then trace the big letter and the little letter right on the card with your finger, a stylus or the mouse — and circle ice cream. Press Save my work when you are proud: your drawing stays here for next time.

    THE LETTER SOUND

    What does I say?

    “i — ie, ice cream starts with I’s name sound”

    Ice cream starts with I’s name sound: ie. The little i also has a short ih sound, as in insect — for now, meet the long ie of ice, the one your child already says when they shout ice cream!

    The little i also says its short ih sound, as in insect. Ice cream meets the long ie first — the one children already know.

    TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

    Ice cream shop.

    Two minutes is plenty. Follow your child’s lead and stop while it is still fun — that is the whole method.

      Open an ice cream shop with paper scoops and a wooden spoon for a scoop.

    2. 02

      Every order starts with ie, ie, ice cream!

    3. 03

      Pay for each cone with a hug — the shop accepts nothing else.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson opens the alphabet at the friendliest door: your child names the letter A, hears its aaaa sound inside a word they eat every week, and traces their very first letters.

    What is this?

    A is the first letter of the alphabet. Big A and little a make the aaaa sound — the one at the start of apple, ant and apron... well, apron comes later; today is the aaaa in apple.

    What does it mean?

    Letters are pictures of sounds, and A is where that idea is born. Your child already owns the word apple; the lesson simply clips a sound and a shape onto something familiar, which is the gentlest possible start.

    What does the child need to know?

    Two things today: the letter is called A, and in apple it says aaaa — the open mouth sound. Big A and little a are the same letter in two sizes, and both can be traced with one finger.

    Why this matters

    Starting with a word your child can taste turns the alphabet from abstract to edible. The name-versus-sound distinction, planted gently now, prevents a year of muddled phonics later.

    What it teaches

    Letter recognition in two cases, sound isolation (the first sound in a word), finger-tracing pre-writing skills, snack-time turn-taking, and the confidence of starting the alphabet with a win.

    Words to learn

    Aapplesoundnametracefirst

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter A — hello, A! And this is an apple. A is the letter’s name, like yours. The sound A makes in apple is aaaa — open your mouth wide and try it: aaaa-apple! Now trace the big A for me, and the little a. Lovely. You just started the whole alphabet."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say both facts slowly: this is the letter A — and this is an apple. Two names for two things on one card.
    2. Make the sound with the mouth wide: aaaa, like the doctor asking you to say ahh. Let your child watch your jaw drop open.
    3. Trace big A with one finger — slide down, slide down, cross the middle — then little a: around and down. Air-tracing counts.
    4. Play the snack game: set out an apple, a banana and a cracker, and ask which one starts with aaaa. The bite is the prize.
    5. Close by hunting: find three things in the room whose names start with the aaaa sound — arm, animal, anything — and give A a wave goodbye.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase A and the little lowercase a on the card, then the shiny apple and the word Apple underneath. Trace each letter with one finger — the card is your child’s first tracing sheet.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What does A say in apple?" "Can you trace the big A?" "Which snack starts with aaaa?" — four questions, answered with a name, a sound, a finger-slide and a happy bite.

    What your child can say or do

    "A! Aaaa-apple!" Expect ahh-sounds at the dinner table, A-spotted on shop signs and cereal boxes, and air-letters drawn in the bath steam. The snack game will be requested daily — A is a delicious letter.

    Out in the real world

    A turns up everywhere: on shop signs, food boxes, the first letter of names. Every spotting is a rerun — name the letter, make the aaaa sound — and snack time is the standing practice ground.

    Try it together

    Sound basket: put four objects on the table — one starting with aaaa (an apple or a toy ant), three that do not. Your child picks the aaaa one, says aaaa aloud, and earns the right to arrange the rest.

    Understanding check

    Ask tomorrow what A says: "aaaa!" with a wide-open mouth means the sound landed. Tracing a little a in the air on request seals the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Keep name and sound clearly separate — "A is its name, aaaa is what it says in apple" said once per session is plenty. Two letters a day is the ceiling; one is better, and stopping while it is still fun is the rule.

    Staying safe

    Snack games need allergy awareness — check for reactions before playing with food, and keep bites sitting-down bites. Nothing else about this card bites back.

    This lesson pairs with the Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson puts B straight into the body: your child pops their lips for the b sound, bounces a ball on every b, and traces their way around the roundest letter pair there is.

    What is this?

    B is the second letter of the alphabet. Big B and little b make the b sound — a quick pop made by pressing the lips together and letting them spring open.

    What does it mean?

    B is one of the sounds children can literally feel — lips together, pop. Sounds with a body-feeling stick fastest, and B’s feeling comes with a ball attached.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called B; the sound is a clean quick b — say it short, without dragging an uuu behind it. B and d look like mirror twins and get mixed up for years; that is normal, not a problem to fix today.

    Why this matters

    A sound your child can make, feel and bounce is unforgettably physical. And the early B-d mix-up is worth knowing about calmly in advance, so it never becomes a worry for either of you.

    What it teaches

    Mouth-muscle awareness (lips pop, voice hums), letter recognition in two cases, sound-and-action pairing, throwing-catching gross motor work, and first sound-hunting in everyday words.

    Words to learn

    Bballbouncelipspopsound

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter B — hello, B! B says b, like a tiny pop. Lips together... pop it open: b! Can you feel your lips do it? Now trace the big B with me — down, bump, bump — and the little b. Every time we bounce the ball, we say b. Ready? Bounce... b!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and introduce the pair: this is the letter B, and this is a ball — say both, then bounce an imaginary one.
    2. Make the sound clean: press your lips together and pop them open — b! Short and neat. Try b three times, quieter each time.
    3. Trace big B — stick down first, then two bumps — and little b: a tall stick with one belly. Your child’s finger does the writing.
    4. Bounce and say: every time the ball hits the floor, out comes the b sound. Bounce-catch-b — the sound lands with the ball.
    5. End with a b-hunt around the house: bubble bath, bread, a bear — collect three b things by pointing and naming.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase B and the little lowercase b on the card, then the ball and the word Ball. Ask which letter is taller — B stands on the line, little b hangs from a stick that reaches up.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does B make?" "Can you feel your lips pop?" "What b-words can we find in this room?" — answered with a name, a clean b, a lip-touch and an enthusiastic hunt.

    What your child can say or do

    "B! B-b-b-ball!" Expect lip-pops at strangers’ names, b-sounds attached to every bounced object, and B announced on buses and birthday cards. Bouncing and b may become permanently married. That is the plan working.

    Out in the real world

    B starts half of childhood: ball, bath, banana, bubble, bath, bed. Every b-word at home is a chance to make the pop — and buses and bats outside are free sightings all day long.

    Try it together

    Bounce counting: bounce the ball five times, one b sound per bounce, then let your child bounce while you supply the sounds. Swap roles — being the sound-person is the phonics practice; being the bouncer is the reward.

    Understanding check

    Ask what B says: a quick clean b with lips popping means the sound is honest and installed. A little b traced in the air completes the pair.

    Parent tips

    If the b gains a trailing uuu (buh), model the short version without correcting — "listen: b!" — and carry on. Keep the bounce game to soft balls and safe floors; the sound survives a missed catch.

    Staying safe

    Bouncing needs ceiling clearance and no breakables in the arc — hallway or outdoors is best. Balls stay out of faces, and the game ends before frustration turns a phonics lesson into a protest.

    This lesson pairs with the Ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Cat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson prowls: your child makes the k click at the back of their mouth, creeps around the room like a cat saying it softly, and traces the letter that is basically a smile.

    What is this?

    C is the third letter of the alphabet. In cat, it makes the k sound — a quick click at the back of the mouth. C is a letter of two talents: it can also borrow the s sound, but cat keeps it simple.

    What does it mean?

    C teaches children that letters share — the same sound as k, wearing a different costume. Accepting that calmly at three makes phonics feel like a game of twins rather than a list of exceptions.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called C; in cat it says k — a clean click, no uuu attached. K and C make the same sound and that is simply true; a shrug and "letters share sounds" is the whole explanation needed at this age.

    Why this matters

    Cat is a word most three-year-olds already say with feeling. Clipping the k sound onto a beloved animal gives C a friendly face — and the prowl game gives the sound a whole body to live in.

    What it teaches

    Back-of-mouth sound production, letter recognition in two cases, soft-versus-loud voice control, crawling coordination, and the sharing-sounds idea that prepares later letters.

    Words to learn

    Ccatclicksoundprowlwhisper

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter C — hello, C! In cat, C says k: a little click at the back of your mouth. Say it with me — k! Now be a cat with me: creep along the floor, soft and quiet... k, k, cat! And when we stand up, we trace the big C and the little c. Round and open, like a smile."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name both: this is the letter C, and this is a cat. Say cat slowly and let the k sound be heard at the front.
    2. Make the k click: the tongue taps the back of the mouth — k! Try k-k-k, like a tick-tock with a cough. Keep it short and clean.
    3. Trace big C — one open curve, like a half-moon — and little c, the same curve smaller. It is the easiest letter to draw in the air.
    4. Prowl: creep around the room on hands and knees, whispering k, k, cat! Whispers make prowling official and keep the game gentle.
    5. End with a k-hunt: find two things that start with the k sound — a toy cat counts, so does a key, a cuddly koala, a kettle.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase C and the little lowercase c, then the cat and the word Cat. Ask which letter looks like it is opening its mouth — C curves open like a cat about to meow.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What does C say in cat?" "Can you make the k click?" "What k-words are hiding in this room?" — answered with a name, a click, a tongue-tap and two finds at least.

    What your child can say or do

    "K! K-k-cat!" Expect clicking sounds in the supermarket, cat-prowling at bathtime, and C spotted on mugs and coats. The whisper-prowl may become the household’s official way to cross a room at night.

    Out in the real world

    C opens cat, cup, car, cake, cold — most of a day’s vocabulary. Every k-sound word is a chance for the click, and every real cat met is the card coming to life at arm’s length.

    Try it together

    Cat prowl and freeze: prowl and whisper k sounds until you call "nap time!" — then every cat curls up still. Reverse roles so your child calls the nap; being the caller is the vocabulary reward.

    Understanding check

    Ask what C says in cat: a clean k click means the sound landed true. A traced C curve in the air completes the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Do not chase the why-does-C-sound-like-K question — "letters like to share sounds" said cheerfully settles it for this year. Keep the prowl to clear floors; knees and table legs negotiate poorly.

    Staying safe

    Prowling happens on open floor, away from stairs and furniture corners. If a real cat joins the game, gentle-hands rules apply: one soft stroke, no tail-pulling, and walking away when the cat says so.

    This lesson pairs with the Cat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Dog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson marches: your child taps the d sound with their tongue, drums it on their knees, joins a barking dog parade, and traces the letter with the big round belly.

    What is this?

    D is the fourth letter of the alphabet. Big D and little d make the d sound — the tongue taps behind the top teeth once and the word is off: d-d-dog.

    What does it mean?

    D comes with its own sound effect — most children bark long before they read. The lesson builds on that enthusiasm and adds the two things a letter lesson needs: the clean sound and the traced shape.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called D; the sound is a quick tongue-tap: d. Say it short and neat, without an uuu trailing behind. B is the lip-pop, D is the tongue-tap — same family, different tools.

    Why this matters

    A letter that arrives with marching, drumming and woofing turns practice into a parade. And feeling the difference between the lip sound and the tongue sound is real phonemic awareness, earned through play.

    What it teaches

    Tongue placement awareness, sound-and-action pairing, rhythm and marching, letter recognition in two cases, and pretend play that doubles as rehearsal — every woof is a d-word in costume.

    Words to learn

    Ddogtaptonguedrumwoof

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter D — hello, D! D says d: your tongue taps behind your teeth, quick like this — d! Feel it tap? Now trace big D with me — tall stick, big belly — and little d. Then we march: d, d, d, and WOOF at the corners. Dogs spell their own letter, honestly."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and greet both: this is the letter D, and this is a dog — say dog and let the d tap at the front of it.
    2. Make the sound: tongue taps behind the top teeth — d! Quick and clean. Now drum it: d-d-d on your knees like a tiny drumroll.
    3. Trace big D — tall stick first, then the big round belly — and little d: a tall stick with a round belly at the bottom.
    4. Start the dog parade: march around the room, one d for every step — d, d, d — with a woof at every corner.
    5. End with the d-hunt: find three things that start with the d sound — a door, a doll, a duck if you have one — and tap each one with the sound.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase D and the little lowercase d on the card, then the dog and the word Dog. Ask which letter has the round belly and which way it faces — D wears its belly on the right.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does D make?" "Where does your tongue tap?" "What d-words can we find on our parade?" — answered with a name, a clean d, a tongue-point and three collected treasures.

    What your child can say or do

    "D! D-d-dog!" Expect knee-drumming at dinner, d-sounds attached to doors and dads, and parades organised at short notice. Woofs may punctuate the alphabet song from now on — accept them as authentic.

    Out in the real world

    D is everywhere a child is: dog, daddy, door, duck, down. Each d-word is a tap rehearsal, and every real dog met on a lead is the card walking past on four legs.

    Try it together

    Drum the sound: tap d-d-d slowly on your knees, then faster, then loud, then whisper-quiet — the sound gets a whole volume range. End with three d-taps on three d-objects you collected.

    Understanding check

    Ask what D says: a quick tongue-tap d means the sound is clean and in place. A big-bellied D traced in the air finishes the lesson.

    Parent tips

    If d slides into buh-land, model the short tap — "d!" — and let your child copy the length, not hear a lecture. B and d mix-ups coming soon are normal; more marching, less testing.

    Staying safe

    Parades need clear floor and walking feet — marching is not sprinting. If a real dog joins the family day, greetings happen with a grown-up close: hand out flat, let the dog come to you, and never bother one that is eating or sleeping.

    This lesson pairs with the Dog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Elephant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson stomps: your child hears the eh sound hiding twice inside one enormous word, swings an arm like a trunk, and traces a letter built from straight lines and shelves.

    What is this?

    E is the fifth letter of the alphabet. In elephant, it makes its short sound: eh — the sound at the start of egg and elbow. Stretch the word out — eh-leh-fant — and the sound turns up twice.

    What does it mean?

    Elephant is a long word wrapped around a short sound, and children love the contrast: the littlest-looking letter in front of the biggest animal on the card. Contrast like that is a memory hook.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called E; in elephant it says eh — mouth relaxed, barely open, a short flat sound. E has other sounds waiting in later years, but today one honest eh is the whole portion.

    Why this matters

    A word your child can hear the sound in twice doubles the practice inside a single word. And a giant animal makes the smallest letter on the card impossible to ignore.

    What it teaches

    Short-vowel sound isolation, syllable stomping (three stomps for eh-leh-fant), letter recognition in two cases, whole-body slow movement, and the early idea that one letter can work twice in one word.

    Words to learn

    Eelephantehsoundtrunkstomp

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter E — hello, E! And this is an elephant. Listen for the eh hiding inside: eh-leh-fant. Can you hear it twice? Make the sound with me — eh! Now swing your trunk and stomp: eh, eh, elephant. Slow and giant, just like a real one. Then trace the big E for me — down, shelf, shelf, shelf."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and let the size land first: this is the letter E, and this is an elephant — a very big animal with a very small sound.
    2. Make the sound: eh — mouth relaxed, barely open, like the little shrug-sound in eh-oh. Try eh three times, then stretch the word: eh-leh-fant.
    3. Trace big E with one finger — one straight back, then three shelves — and little e: a small curve with a shelf tucked across its middle.
    4. March like an elephant: slow heavy steps, one arm swinging like a trunk, one eh for every stomp. Elephants never hurry, and neither does this letter.
    5. Close with an eh-hunt: find two things whose names start with eh — an egg from the fridge, an elbow, the edge of a rug — and stomp once for each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase E and the little lowercase e on the card, then the elephant and the word Elephant. Ask which letter holds more shelves — big E stacks three, little e keeps one tucked in its curve.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What does E say in elephant?" "How many times can you hear eh in eh-leh-fant?" "Can you take one giant elephant step?" — answered with a name, a short eh, two happy discoveries and one floor-shaking stomp.

    What your child can say or do

    "Eh! Eh-elephant!" Expect trunk-arms at breakfast, eh-sounds offered for eggs and elbows, and very slow crossings of the living room. Elephant may become the preferred way to walk anywhere. The stomping is the lesson working.

    Out in the real world

    E waits quietly in a child’s day: egg, elbow, edge, elephant at the zoo, exit signs on doors. Every eh you spot together is a rerun of the card — name it, sound it, stomp on by.

    Try it together

    Elephant steps: lay three cushions or paper spots on the floor and cross them with slow giant steps, one eh per step. Add a trunk-arm challenge at the far end — pick up a small toy, elephant-style, and carry it back.

    Understanding check

    Ask tomorrow what E says in elephant: a short flat eh means the sound landed. Little e traced in the air — curve first, then shelf — completes the letter.

    Parent tips

    One sound per letter is the rule at this age: eh is today’s whole serving, and E’s name-sound can wait politely for another year. If the march grows too lively, shrink it to trunk-arms only and keep the feet still.

    Staying safe

    Elephant marching needs clear floor and slow feet — the whole point is heaviness, not speed. Cushion-hopping stays low and supervised, and stomping pauses whenever anyone smaller than an elephant is underfoot.

    This lesson pairs with the Elephant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Fish — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson breathes: your child rests top teeth on a bottom lip, lets the air slide out in a clean fff, blows a feather across the table and traces the letter with the tidy shelves.

    What is this?

    F is the sixth letter of the alphabet. Big F and little f make the f sound — a windy whisper made with the top teeth resting on the bottom lip while the air slides out. No voice, just wind.

    What does it mean?

    F is the first soundless sound in the set: nothing buzzes, only air moves. Feeling that quiet — wind with no voice behind it — is real phonemic awareness your child can hold in one long breath.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called F; the sound is fff, long and soft. If a buzz sneaks in, the voice has switched on and v has borrowed the mouth — quiet air means F is being said correctly.

    Why this matters

    A sound your child can see working in a dancing tissue checks itself: wind moves the tissue, buzzing does not. The fish just supplies the swimming story that keeps everyone playing.

    What it teaches

    Lip-teeth placement awareness, voice-off versus voice-on discrimination, breath length control, letter recognition in two cases, and the finger isolation needed for tracing — all inside one quiet game.

    Words to learn

    Ffishfffwindblowquiet

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter F — hello, F! F says fff, like wind slipping out. Teeth on your lip, then blow: fff. Feel it? No voice, just air — the quietest sound in the alphabet. Now we swim: fff, fff, fish! And trace the big F with me — down, shelf, shelf — like a flagpole with two little flags."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and make the introductions: this is the letter F, and this is a fish — the quietest animal in the whole alphabet set.
    2. Make the sound: top teeth rest on the bottom lip and the air slides out — fff. Hold your throat and notice the quiet: no buzz, only wind.
    3. Trace big F — one tall line down, then two shelves across the top — and little f: a tall line with a small hook at the top and one crossbar.
    4. Play the wind game: lay a feather or tissue on the table and move it along with fff puffs — long wind, short wind, then a racing wind.
    5. End with an f-hunt: find three things whose names start with fff — a finger, a foot, a picture of a frog — and blow a little fff at each one.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase F and the little lowercase f on the card, then the fish and the word Fish. Ask which letter carries more shelves — big F has two crossbars, little f wears just one.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does F make?" "Can you feel the wind with no buzz in it?" "What f-words can we blow toward in this room?" — answered with a name, an airy fff, a quiet throat and a wandering finger.

    What your child can say or do

    "Fff! Fff-fish!" Expect lip-teeth experiments at dinner, fff-puffs at candles and dandelions, and wind sounds aimed at everything light enough to move. A quietly blowy child is F’s favourite souvenir.

    Out in the real world

    F floats through the day: fork, flower, foot, fish fingers, the four on the clock. Every fff is one breath long — spot it, say it, and let the air do the teaching.

    Try it together

    Feather race: two players blow a feather or a small paper ball across the table toward each other, every push released as fff. Longest wind wins, not loudest — and the fish card referees from the side.

    Understanding check

    Ask what F says: a long soft fff with the teeth finding the lip means the sound landed. A throat-check with no buzz seals it — quiet air, correct letter.

    Parent tips

    If fff buzzes into vvv, hold your own throat and compare out loud — the quiet one is F — then keep playing; the distinction arrives through feeling, not correction. Wind games stay gentle and well away from eyes.

    Staying safe

    Feathers, tissues and small paper balls stay out of mouths and away from eyes — blowing only, never sucking. Keep puff-play off tables with breakables, and park the game before anyone gets too breathless to laugh.

    This lesson pairs with the Fish flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Grapes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson snacks its way through the letter: your child makes the guh sound at the back of their mouth, counts grapes one guh at a time, and traces a letter with a tail.

    What is this?

    G is the seventh letter of the alphabet. In grapes, it makes its hard sound: guh — the back-of-the-mouth sound at the start of goose and giggle. The throat does the work; the lips stay out of it.

    What does it mean?

    G is a snack-table word, which means the practice renews itself several times a day without a lesson plan in sight. Letters attached to food get more rehearsal than any worksheet could buy.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called G; in grapes it says guh — short and clean, made at the back. G owns a second sound, the j in giant, but grapes keeps today simple: one fruit, one sound.

    Why this matters

    Snacks arrive daily and grapes rarely miss a week, so this card earns more repetitions than almost any other in the set. Frequency, not cleverness, is what makes a letter sound stick.

    What it teaches

    Back-of-mouth sound production, one-to-one counting paired with sound, letter recognition in two cases, pincer-grip snack handling, and the patience of waiting for a counted treat.

    Words to learn

    Ggrapesguhcountsnackbunch

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter G — hello, G! G says guh, right at the back of your mouth, like a tiny gulp. Say it with me — guh, guh, grapes! Now count the plate with me: one guh, two guh, three guh... and eat the counting! Then trace the big G — round and round, with a little tail at the end."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name the pair: this is the letter G, and this is a bunch of grapes — say grapes slowly and let guh stand up at the front.
    2. Make the sound at the back of your mouth: guh, like a gentle gulp. Try guh three times, then guh-grapes, feeling the throat do the work.
    3. Trace big G — a round curve that grows a small tail at the end — and little g: a circle with a tail that dangles below the line.
    4. Count grapes onto a little plate: one guh, two guh, three guh — one sound per grape, then eat the counting one grape at a time.
    5. End with a guh-hunt around the room: a toy goose, a giggle on demand, somebody’s grandpa in a photo — collect three and give each a clean guh.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase G and the little lowercase g on the card, then the bunch of grapes and the word Grapes. Ask which letter grew a tail — big G’s curve ends in a small hook, little g’s tail hangs below.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What does G say in grapes?" "Where do you feel the sound — front or back of your mouth?" "How many grapes shall we count next?" — answered with a name, a back-of-mouth guh, a hand on the throat and a number.

    What your child can say or do

    "Guh! Guh-grapes!" Expect grape-counting requests at snack time, guh-sounds offered to grandparents and garden hoses, and tails added to every circle your child draws. G is the letter that eats its homework.

    Out in the real world

    G grows through daily life: grapes, goose, giggle, gate, grandma. Every guh at the table or the garden gate is the card repeating itself — and snack counters never seem to tire of it.

    Try it together

    Grape counting shop: your child arranges six grape halves on a plate as the shopkeeper, you order one guh, two guh, three guh — and only sound-perfect counting gets the order filled. Swap roles; the shopkeeper may demand payment in guh-sounds.

    Understanding check

    Ask what G says in grapes: a clean back-of-mouth guh means the hard sound landed. A little g traced in the air — circle first, dangling tail second — completes the lesson.

    Parent tips

    G’s j-sound in giant or giraffe can stay a mystery for another year — if it comes up, "G has two costumes; today it wears the grape one" settles it cheerfully. Counted snacks end when the plate is empty, not before.

    Staying safe

    Whole grapes are a choking risk for under-fours — halve them lengthways before any counting game, and keep eating sitting-down. Washed hands, washed grapes, and the game pauses until every mouth is empty.

    This lesson pairs with the Grapes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    House — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson breathes out: your child fogs an imaginary window, makes a tissue dance with a warm hhh, and traces the letter that looks like a ladder between two walls.

    What is this?

    H is the eighth letter of the alphabet. Big H and little h make the h sound — a warm breathy sigh, like fogging a window or warming cold hands. Open mouth, warm air, nothing else.

    What does it mean?

    H is nearly invisible in fast speech — children hear ouse more than they hear the h. This lesson slows the breath down until the sound is something your child can feel on a palm and see in a tissue.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called H; the sound is hhh — pure warm air, no voice, no tap. The mouth stays open and the breath comes out, which is exactly why the sound can disappear when words speed up.

    Why this matters

    A sound your child can see moving a tissue teaches itself: the tissue dances or it does not. And house is already one of the most-rehearsed words in any small child’s day.

    What it teaches

    Breath control and direction, voice-off airflow awareness, letter recognition in two cases, fine finger work for tissue handling, and word-start listening — catching the h at the front of spoken words.

    Words to learn

    Hhousehhhbreathwarmdoor

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter H — hello, H! H says hhh — a warm breath, like fogging up a window. Breathe on your hand: can you feel the warmth? That is the whole sound. Now make the tissue dance for me — hhh, hhh, house! Then trace the big H: two tall walls and a ladder between."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and open the door: this is the letter H, and this is a house — the house your h sound lives in.
    2. Make the sound: breathe out slowly and warmly onto your palm — hhh — the way you would fog a window. Try it three times; the palm should feel warm each time.
    3. Trace big H — two tall walls and one ladder rung between them — and little h: a tall wall that drops into a small hump.
    4. Play the tissue dance: hold a tissue up to your lips, breathe a warm hhh and watch it dance. Then hhh-house, hhh-hat, hhh-hand — three warm breaths around the room.
    5. End with an h-hunt: find three things that start with the breathy sound — a hand, a hat, a head — and breathe a little hhh at each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase H and the little lowercase h on the card, then the house and the word House. Ask which letter looks like a ladder — big H keeps its rung high up, little h melts its wall into a hump.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does H make?" "Can you warm my hand with your hhh?" "What h-words live in this room?" — answered with a name, a warm sigh, a surprised palm and a small expedition.

    What your child can say or do

    "Hhh! Hhh-house!" Expect window-fogging on every cold pane, warm breaths blown onto grown-up hands, and h-sounds offered to hats, horses and hair. The tissue dance will be requested at every meal.

    Out in the real world

    H hides at the start of half a morning: house, hand, hair, hat, hurry up. Each whispered hhh on the way out the door is the card breathing along with your family.

    Try it together

    Warm-breath mirror: press palms together, take turns saying hhh onto each other’s skin and guess whose breath was warmer. Then aim a joint hhh at a tissue until it slides off the table — teamwork, one warm breath at a time.

    Understanding check

    Ask what H says: a warm audible sigh on an open mouth means the sound landed — the classic miss is silence, so listen for real moving air. A little h traced in the air completes the pair.

    Parent tips

    If the h vanishes in fast speech — ouse instead of house — slow the word right down at the front door and let the breath be heard. Exaggeration is the fix; correction is not.

    Staying safe

    Tissues and light objects for breath games stay out of mouths and away from eyes. Window-fogging needs a grown-up nearby so nobody leans on glass, and breath games pause when anyone has a cough.

    This lesson pairs with the House flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Ice cream — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson scoops: your child meets the letter that says its own name out loud, runs an ice cream shop with pom-pom scoops, and traces a letter built like a shelf with a stand.

    What is this?

    I is the ninth letter of the alphabet. In ice cream, it says its own name: ii — exactly the sound from the alphabet song. I owns two sounds; on this card the long name-sound takes the cone.

    What does it mean?

    I is the first letter whose sound is its own name, which makes it oddly easy: your child already says ii every time they sing the alphabet. The card just parks that sound on a dessert.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called I, and in ice cream it also says ii — the same thing twice. Later words will use a short i, like insect; on this card the name-sound wins the treat, and that is honest.

    Why this matters

    Vowels bend, and meeting that idea through a beloved treat keeps it friendly: no rule-memorising, just a letter that sometimes says its name and an ice cream that always says summer.

    What it teaches

    Vowel flexibility met early and gently, letter-name and letter-sound held side by side, letter recognition in two cases, pretend-shop turn-taking, and scoop counting for early maths.

    Words to learn

    Iice creamnamesoundscoopsweet

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter I — hello, I! Listen carefully: in ice cream, I says its own name — ii! Just like in the song. Say it tall and long: iii-ice cream. Now scoop for me — one pom-pom, two pom-pom — and hand it over with an enormous ii! What a treat of a letter."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and set up the surprise: this is the letter I, and this is ice cream — and here I says its own name, which almost no letter gets to do.
    2. Sing the sound: ii — the note I takes in the alphabet song. Hold it like a long note: iii. Then park it at the front of the word: ii-ice cream.
    3. Trace big I — one tall stand with a shelf above and a shelf below — and little i: a short stick with a dot floating over it like a cherry.
    4. Open the ice cream shop: cups, pom-poms or balls for scoops. Every order is called with the sound — ii-ice cream, please! — before any scooping happens.
    5. Close with an ii-hunt: find things whose names start with the name-sound — ice from the freezer, an iron if one lives here, an island on a map — and give each a pretend lick.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase I and the little lowercase i on the card, then the ice cream cone and the word Ice cream. Ask which letter wears a dot — little i carries one above it, like a cherry on top.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What does I say in ice cream?" "Does the letter say its own name here?" "What flavour shall we scoop next?" — answered with a name, a long ii, a delighted yes and an order.

    What your child can say or do

    "Ii! Ii-ice cream!" Expect shop orders shouted across the kitchen, ii-sounds offered to ice cubes and ironing boards, and alphabet-song moments where the I gets a solo. The dot on little i may be explained at length to anyone who stands still.

    Out in the real world

    I turns up chilled: ice cubes in drinks, ice lollies in the freezer, icing on a cake. Every ii is the name-sound saying hello — spot it together and the alphabet song gains a meaning.

    Try it together

    Scoop shop: three cups, a pom-pom pile and one rule — every order must begin with a long ii before any scooping. Swap customer and shopkeeper; the customer pays in sounds, the shopkeeper invents flavours.

    Understanding check

    Ask what I says in ice cream: a long name-sound ii means the honest vowel fact landed. A little i traced in the air — stick first, dot second — completes the treat.

    Parent tips

    Keep both facts light: "I has two sounds; today it says its own name" is the whole explanation, and short i can wait for insects. Never quiz the distinction — the alphabet song teaches it for free.

    Staying safe

    Scooping stays pretend — pom-poms and balls are not food and small parts stay away from little siblings. If real ice cream joins the lesson, check for allergies first and keep eating sitting down.

    This lesson pairs with the Ice cream flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Juice — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson toasts: your child makes the juh sound that hops off the tongue, clinks two little cups on every juh, and traces a letter with a hook like a fisherman’s.

    What is this?

    J is the tenth letter of the alphabet. Big J and little j make the j sound — a quick jumping juh, like the start of jump and jam. The voice hops once and the word is away.

    What does it mean?

    Juice is a requested-by-name word in most households, which hands this card a rehearsal slot at breakfast every day. Letters that live inside routines need almost no extra teaching.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called J; the sound is a quick juh — say it short, with no uuu dragged along behind. J is a young letter with a short history and one clear job your child can master today.

    Why this matters

    A sound that jumps pairs perfectly with a toast game: clink, juh, sip. Rhythm plus routine plus refreshment is the strongest trio in the set — breakfast does the revising for you.

    What it teaches

    Quick-release sound production, turn-taking with cups, letter recognition in two cases, gentle pouring and clinking coordination, and the routine-attachment that makes practice happen by itself.

    Words to learn

    Jjuicejuhjumpcupcheers

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter J — hello, J! J says juh — a quick jump of a sound, like the start of jump. Say it with me: juh, juh, juice! Now pour the cups, clink them on the juh, and drink. Cheers! You just toasted the whole letter."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at breakfast if you can: this is the letter J, and this is juice — the word your child already orders by name.
    2. Make the sound: juh, quick and springy, like the start of jump. Say juh-juh-jump and let the sound hop each time.
    3. Trace big J — a tall line that hooks to the left at the bottom — and little j: a shorter line with its hook and a dot floating above.
    4. Pour two small cups and toast: clink on the juh — juh, juh, juice! — then both take a sip. Three toasts is a full round.
    5. End with a juh-hunt: find three j-things — a jacket on its hook, a jar lid, a toy jeep — and hop once for each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase J and the little lowercase j on the card, then the juice box and the word Juice. Ask which letter wears a dot — little j carries one above its hook, big J goes bareheaded.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does J make?" "Can you hop on the juh?" "What j-words can we find before breakfast ends?" — answered with a name, a springy juh, one hop and a proud point.

    What your child can say or do

    "Juh! Juh-juice!" Expect toast-clinking at every meal, juh-sounds offered to jackets and jelly, and hops inserted mid-word for emphasis. Juice requests may officially become juh requests. Accept the upgrade.

    Out in the real world

    J pours itself daily: juice at breakfast, jam on toast, jump in the garden, jelly at parties. Each juh at the table is the card repeating its lesson while everyone is busy drinking.

    Try it together

    Cups up: two small cups, one rule — nobody drinks until the toast is said, and the toast must start with a clean juh. Vary the volume: giant juh, tiny juh, whisper juh. The silliest toast wins the first sip.

    Understanding check

    Ask what J says: a quick springy juh with no trailing uuu means the sound landed. A little j traced in the air — hook first, dot second — finishes the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Keep the juh short and the toasts many — sound length is the whole lesson here. If breakfast runs late, the cups can be empty; the clink and the sound are the point, not the drink.

    Staying safe

    Pouring stays small and supervised — a splash of water works as well as juice. Cups are unbreakable, clinking stays gentle, sipping waits until everyone is seated, and no one runs, jumps or juggles with cups.

    This lesson pairs with the Juice flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Kite — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson runs: your child taps the k sound at the back of their mouth, sprints with arms raised like kite string, and meets the letter that shares its sound with C.

    What is this?

    K is the eleventh letter of the alphabet. It makes the k sound — the same quick click at the back of the mouth that C makes in cat. Two letters, one sound; English shares them around.

    What does it mean?

    K is the second letter to arrive with a sound your child already owns. Meeting that as a game of twins — C and K sharing one sound like friends sharing a bike — keeps it friendly for life.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called K; the sound is kuh, the clean back-of-mouth click. Silent-k words like knife and know are strictly off the menu today — today K flies a kite and that is all.

    Why this matters

    Kites mean wind, running and a grown-up holding the string, so this card unlocks an outing, not just a lesson. And hearing cat’s sound come out of kite plants the sharing idea early and painlessly.

    What it teaches

    Back-of-mouth click production, sound-sharing awareness, letter recognition in two cases, whole-body sprinting with quick direction changes, and arm-up postural play that doubles as kite pretending.

    Words to learn

    Kkitekuhwindrunstring

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter K — hello, K! K says kuh — the click at the back of your mouth, the very same one C uses in cat. Try it: kuh, kuh, kite! Now be a kite: arms up, string tight, and run! When the wind drops, we trace the big K — tall line, then kick, kick."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and look up: this is the letter K, and this is a kite — high up, holding on to its string.
    2. Make the click: tongue taps the back of the mouth — kuh! The same sound cat’s C uses. Try kuh three times, then kuh-kite.
    3. Trace big K — one tall line, then a small arm reaching out and a leg kicking away — and little k: a tall line with a small arm and a tucked leg.
    4. Run like a kite: arms up holding invisible string, dashing across the garden or hallway, one kuh for every burst of speed.
    5. End with a k-hunt: find three things that start with the k sound — the toy cat from the C lesson, a key, a picture of a king — and click the sound at each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase K and the little lowercase k on the card, then the kite and the word Kite. Ask which letters look ready to move — both Ks reach away from their tall line with arms and a leg.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does K make?" "Which other letter makes this exact sound?" "Can you run like a kite for three kuh-steps?" — answered with a name, a click, a proud C and a dash across the grass.

    What your child can say or do

    "Kuh! Kuh-kite!" Expect arm-up sprinting in open spaces, k-sounds offered to keys and kicks, and C-K friendships declared over breakfast. The toy cat may be promoted to honorary K. The sharing idea has landed.

    Out in the real world

    K clicks quietly through the day: key, kick, kitchen, ketchup, kites at the park. Every click is a rerun — and every shared kuh with a cat or a car seat is the twins idea still working.

    Try it together

    Kite string dash: tie a light ribbon to a stick and run with it streaming behind, one shouted kuh per straight stretch. When you call wind down, the kite lands in a crouch — then relaunches on the next kuh.

    Understanding check

    Ask what K says: a clean back-of-mouth click means the sound landed — bonus points if your child names C as the sound-sharer. A little k traced in the air completes the pair.

    Parent tips

    Resist explaining silent-k words — knife and know can wait years. If the C-K question comes up, "letters share sounds like friends share toys" said once, cheerfully, is the whole curriculum for today.

    Staying safe

    Kite-running needs open space, clear of furniture corners and garden hazards, with shoes on and eyes on the ground rather than the sky. Ribbon games stay far from necks, and real kite string is a grown-up’s job.

    This lesson pairs with the Kite flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Lion — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson roars: your child lifts their tongue tip for a sound they can actually watch happening, switches between lion-loud and cub-quiet, and traces a letter shaped like a corner.

    What is this?

    L is the twelfth letter of the alphabet. Big L and little l make the l sound — lll, made by tapping the tongue tip just behind the top teeth. It is the most visible sound in the whole set.

    What does it mean?

    L can be watched: sit side by side with a mirror and the tongue lift is unmistakable. Seeing a sound removes all guesswork — the mouth shows its own homework, and the giggles come free.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called L; the sound is lll — tongue tip up, voice on. Hold it and it lasts as long as breath allows. The roar is optional theatre; the tongue tap is the actual lesson.

    Why this matters

    A sound that can be seen, held and scaled from roar to whisper gives one letter three games. And lion comes with the most requested sound effect in childhood, which this card happily spends.

    What it teaches

    Tongue-tip placement awareness, mirror self-observation, volume scaling from loud to whisper, letter recognition in two cases, and held-sound breath control that helps every later letter too.

    Words to learn

    Llionllltongueroarmirror

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter L — hello, L! L says lll — tongue tip up, right behind your teeth. Look in the mirror: can you see your tongue? Hold it — lllll — and let it roar: LLL! Now whisper like a cub... lll. Lovely and loud, then lovely and quiet. That is the whole lion."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and announce the star: this is the letter L, and this is a lion — the loudest helper in the alphabet box.
    2. Make the sound in a mirror: the tongue tip taps the ridge just behind your top teeth — lll. Watch your own tongue lift, then let your child catch theirs doing it.
    3. Trace big L — one tall line down and one short foot across the bottom — and little l: a single tall stick, the simplest letter there is.
    4. Play the three moods: roar like a big lion with a huge lll, whisper like a cub with a tiny one, then yawn like a sleepy lion with a slow one.
    5. End with an l-hunt: find three things whose names start with lll — a lemon, a ladle from the kitchen drawer, a leaf from a plant — and tap the sound onto each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase L and the little lowercase l on the card, then the lion and the word Lion. Ask which letter is simpler to draw — little l is one straight stick, big L adds a foot at the bottom.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does L make?" "Can you see your tongue in the mirror?" "Show me lion-loud, then cub-quiet" — answered with a name, a tongue-tip lll, a delighted grin and a volume change.

    What your child can say or do

    "Lll! Lll-lion!" Expect mirror-tongue inspections after every tooth-brushing, roars in corridors and whispers in libraries, and l-sounds offered to lemons and lamps. The three-moods game may run at bedtime indefinitely.

    Out in the real world

    L lifts its tongue all day: leaf, lunch, lamp, lip, the big L of lorries passing. Every lll is visible if you look — and every real lion met, at a zoo or in a book, is the card roaring back.

    Try it together

    Mirror lion: sit side by side at a mirror, open wide and take turns showing your lll tongues — loudest lion, longest lll, silliest lion face. The mirror never lies, and the tongue lift becomes unmistakable in one sitting.

    Understanding check

    Ask what L says: an lll with the tongue tip visibly up means the sound landed — the mirror settles any doubt. A tall little l traced in the air finishes the letter.

    Parent tips

    If the tongue stays down, model it in the mirror rather than explaining — watching beats telling at this age. Keep roaring to rooms that can take it, and let the whisper version rescue quiet times.

    Staying safe

    Mirror play happens seated or standing still, never running past glass. Roaring stays at indoor-safe volume near small siblings and sleeping households, and lion pouncing is for cushions, not for pets or people.

    This lesson pairs with the Lion flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Moon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hums: your child closes their lips and holds the mmm for as long as breath allows, hunts the real moon out of the window, and traces a letter full of mountain peaks.

    What is this?

    M is the thirteenth letter of the alphabet. Big M and little m make the m sound — mmm, a hum made with lips together and the voice switched on. It lasts exactly as long as your breath does.

    What does it mean?

    M is the easiest sound in the set to feel and the hardest to miss: lips closed, hum out. Attach it to the moon and the practice renews itself every clear night, right at the calmest hour.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called M; the sound is mmm — closed lips, humming voice, no burst of air. Hold it long, hold it short, taste something delicious with it: the hum stays the same throughout.

    Why this matters

    A bedtime word means bedtime practice, and no other card lands at a calmer hour. The mmm contest turns breath control into a game, and the moon turns the sky into a flashcard that comes out nightly.

    What it teaches

    Humming with closed lips, breath-length control, letter recognition in two cases, sky observation and pointing, and the evening-routine attachment that lets this card teach itself after dark.

    Words to learn

    Mmoonmmmhumlipsnight

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter M — hello, M! M says mmm — lips together, and hum like you have tasted something wonderful. Feel your lips buzz? Hold it — mmmm. Now look up: that is the moon. Say it with me — mmm-moon! Good night, moon. Good night, M."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card in the evening if you can: this is the letter M, and this is the moon — the letter’s favourite address in the sky.
    2. Make the sound with lips closed: hum — mmm. Feel the tickle behind your lips. Try one long mmm, then three short ones.
    3. Trace big M — down, peak up, valley down, peak up, down — and little m: one short stick followed by two small humps.
    4. Play the mmm contest: everyone hums with lips closed and the longest hum wins. Then hum through some words — mmm-moon, mmm-mummy, mmm-milk.
    5. End at the window: hunt the moon out of the sky together and greet it with mmm-moon! If there is a crescent up there, trace its curve with one finger.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase M and the little lowercase m on the card, then the moon and the word Moon. Ask which letter has more peaks — big M climbs two mountain peaks, little m rolls two gentle humps.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does M make?" "How long can you hold your mmm?" "Can you find the moon from here?" — answered with a name, a closed-lip hum, a breath-length record and a pointing finger.

    What your child can say or do

    "Mmm! Mmm-moon!" Expect humming at every delicious meal, m-sounds offered to mummies and milkshakes, and moon-inspection at every bedtime from now on. The mmm contest may crown a permanent family champion.

    Out in the real world

    M hums through the whole day: milk, mummy, more, moon at bedtime. Every closed-lip hum is the card rehearsing itself — and the real moon keeps the appointment every clear night for free.

    Try it together

    mmm contest: faces together, lips closed, one long hum each — longest breath wins and chooses tonight’s bedtime story. Then hum the word moon together as the lights go down: the calmest phonics game ever devised.

    Understanding check

    Ask what M says: a closed-lip hum that holds and stretches means the sound landed perfectly. A little m traced in the air — stick, hump, hump — completes the evening.

    Parent tips

    This is the gentlest card in the set — save it for tired evenings. If the hum escapes into a muh with lips apart, close your own lips pointedly and hum; copying your face does the rest without a word of correction.

    Staying safe

    Moon-spotting happens from a window, balcony or doorway with a grown-up present — never leaning out. Keep the mmm contest to calm volumes after bedtime, and save crescent-drawing for indoors paper.

    This lesson pairs with the Moon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Nest — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson settles in: your child feels the nnn buzz in their nose, builds a pretend nest big enough to sit in, and discovers that N and M are humming twins with different lips.

    What is this?

    N is the fourteenth letter of the alphabet. Big N and little n make the n sound — nnn, lips shut with a gentle tingle buzzing in the nose. The tongue rises to make it; the lips stay closed.

    What does it mean?

    N is a nose sound, which makes it instantly findable: feel the tingle. And nest is a word with a build-it game attached, so this letter comes with furniture included.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called N; the sound is nnn — lips closed, tongue up, nose buzzing. M and n are the humming twins: mmm closes with both lips, nnn hums with only the tongue lifted. One mirror moment settles it.

    Why this matters

    A sound your child can feel in the nose and a word they can physically sit inside makes this card a rainy-day favourite. The M-N comparison, done gently, prevents years of letter confusion.

    What it teaches

    Nasal sound awareness, tongue-versus-lip discrimination against M, letter recognition in two cases, cushion-and-blanket construction play, and whisper-voice control for indoor nest sitting.

    Words to learn

    Nnestnnnnosebirdsnug

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter N — hello, N! N says nnn — lips closed, tongue up, and your nose tingles. Feel it buzzing? Now say it softly: nnn, nnn, nest. Shall we build one? Cushions here, blanket there... climb in, little bird. Nnn-nest. Cosy, isn’t it?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and introduce the home: this is the letter N, and this is a nest — a bird’s bed, made of sticks and built high in a tree.
    2. Make the sound: lips closed, tongue lifts — nnn. Feel the tingle in your nose. Try nnn three times, then nnn-nest.
    3. Trace big N — one tall line down, a diagonal slide, another tall line — and little n: a short stick with one doorway hump.
    4. Build the nest: cushions and blankets arranged together, then climb inside like a bird settling down and whisper nnn, nnn, nest.
    5. End with an n-hunt: find three n-things — a nut from the kitchen, a toy nail, your own nose — and buzz the sound at each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase N and the little lowercase n on the card, then the nest and the word Nest. Ask how the letters differ from M — big N has a slide in the middle, and little n wears one hump where m wears two.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does N make?" "Where do you feel the tingle?" "Can you build a nest for your toy bird?" — answered with a name, a nose-buzz, a pointing finger and a cushion arrangement.

    What your child can say or do

    "Nnn! Nnn-nest!" Expect nose-tingling announcements, n-sounds offered to bananas and naps, and cushion nests appearing in the living room without warning. Toy birds may be tucked in nightly. The snuggle is the lesson holding.

    Out in the real world

    N hums quietly through the day: nap, nose, noodles, nine, the night-night at bedtime. Every tongue-up hum is the card again — and any real nest spotted on a walk is the word standing in a tree, made of sticks.

    Try it together

    Nest builders: gather cushions, blankets and a laundry basket into a snug corner nest, climb in and take turns whispering nnn-words — nest, nap, night-night. The quietest bird gets the softest cushion; loud birds relocate politely.

    Understanding check

    Ask what N says: a tongue-up hum with lips closed means the sound landed — check that it is nnn, not mmm, by watching the lips. A little n traced in the air completes the nest.

    Parent tips

    If N slides into M, do not lecture — sit at a mirror once, hum both sounds and let your child watch which one lifts the tongue. One comparison a week is plenty; mix-ups here are normal and temporary.

    Staying safe

    Nest-building keeps cushions away from stair edges and never stacks higher than safe climbing. Blankets stay loose enough to breathe easily, and the game includes climbing out on request — no tucked-in birds without consent.

    This lesson pairs with the Nest flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Orange — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson peels: your child rounds their mouth into a little o for the sound, traces circles on the fruit before it opens, and counts segments while the room fills with the smell.

    What is this?

    O is the fifteenth letter of the alphabet. In orange, it makes its short round sound: oh — the sound at the start of on and octopus. Your mouth makes a little O shape to say it.

    What does it mean?

    O is the letter that draws itself: round the lips, round the fruit, round the letter. A shape repeated three ways in one lesson feels like discovery every single time.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called O; in orange it says oh — short and round, mouth open in a small circle. O has other sounds in other words, but today the orange keeps things simple and peelable.

    Why this matters

    Smell is the strongest memory hook there is, and this card arrives with one built in. Peeling, counting and sharing segments turns the letter into snack time, which is where practice sticks best.

    What it teaches

    Round-lip sound production, circle tracing in air and on surfaces, letter recognition in two cases, pincer-grip peeling and segment-pulling, and one-to-one counting that ends in sharing.

    Words to learn

    Oorangeohroundpeelshare

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter O — hello, O! O says oh — make your mouth a little circle, like this: oh. Look, your lips just drew the letter! Now smell the orange... peel it with me... count the pieces: oh, oh, oh! Round and sweet, just like the letter."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and pass the fruit if you have one: this is the letter O, and this is an orange — round, like the letter itself.
    2. Make the sound with a small round mouth: oh. Watch your lips draw a little O in the mirror. Try oh three times, then oh-orange.
    3. Trace big O — one round loop, all the way around — and little o: the same circle, smaller. Draw both in the air, then on the orange’s skin.
    4. Peel together: pull the skin away in pieces, break the fruit into segments and count them out — one oh, two oh, three oh.
    5. End with an oh-hunt: find three round things or oh-words — a ball, a bowl, an octopus toy if one lives here — and trace a circle above each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase O and the little lowercase o on the card, then the orange and the word Orange. Ask what shape both letters make — one closed loop, big and small, the easiest circle in the alphabet.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What does O say in orange?" "Can your mouth make the letter’s shape?" "How many segments shall we count this time?" — answered with a name, a round oh, a circle-mouth and a number.

    What your child can say or do

    "Oh! Oh-orange!" Expect circle-mouths in mirrors, oh-sounds offered to onions and octopuses, and segment-counting at every orange until further notice. The smell will summon the lesson from another room. That is the plan working.

    Out in the real world

    O rolls through the day: orange at snack time, on and open and over in speech, circles everywhere your child looks. Every round thing is a tracing prompt and every peeled fruit is the card, refreshed.

    Try it together

    Segment shop: peel an orange, lay the segments in a row and count them aloud with an oh per piece. Then share them out — one for you, one for me — trading every handover with an oh. Maths, phonics and manners in one fruit.

    Understanding check

    Ask what O says in orange: a short round oh with circle lips means the sound landed. A little o traced in the air — one smooth loop, no corners — completes the fruit bowl.

    Parent tips

    Let the circle do the teaching: lips, fruit, letter, loop drawn in the air — the shape repeats itself without any drilling. If other O sounds come up in books, smile and save them; the orange owns this week.

    Staying safe

    Peeling starts with grown-up hands for the first cut, then small fingers pull the loosened skin. Segments are cut to suit your child’s chewing stage, and sticky hands get washed before anything else is touched.

    This lesson pairs with the Orange flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Pig — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson puffs: your child releases a tiny explosion of air strong enough to move a tissue, trots around the room with an oink in reserve, and traces a letter shaped like B’s cousin.

    What is this?

    P is the sixteenth letter of the alphabet. Big P and little p make the p sound — puh, a tiny puff of air that pops out from closed lips. No buzz, just the little gust.

    What does it mean?

    P is B’s twin: same lips, but B buzzes and P only breathes. Children mix the two freely and it costs nothing — the tissue test makes the difference visible whenever anyone is curious.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called P; the sound is puh, a short puff. Say it with a tissue in front of your mouth and the tissue jumps — that little gust is the entire sound, and oinks are optional garnish.

    Why this matters

    A sound your child can see working in a jumping tissue turns correction into observation: it either moved or it did not. And the pig supplies the giggle track that keeps everyone coming back.

    What it teaches

    Lip-burst airflow control, voice-off versus voice-on discrimination against B, letter recognition in two cases, trotting gross-motor play, and pretend feeding games that grow vocabulary on the side.

    Words to learn

    Ppigpuhpufftissueoink

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter P — hello, P! P says puh — a tiny puff of air, like this. Lips together... pop! See the tissue jump? That is the whole sound. Now trot with me: puh, puh, pig! Oink optional but encouraged. Then we trace the big P — tall stick, round belly."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and make the introduction: this is the letter P, and this is a pig — the noisiest dinner guest in the barnyard.
    2. Make the puff: lips together, then let a tiny gust pop out — puh. Hold a tissue in front of your mouth and watch it jump each time.
    3. Trace big P — a tall stick with a belly attached at the top — and little p: the same shape with its belly hanging below the line.
    4. Play the trot: hands and knees or trotting feet, moving through the room saying puh, puh, pig — with an oink at every corner.
    5. End with a p-hunt: find three things that start with the puff sound — a pot, a pencil, a pet picture — and puff the sound at each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase P and the little lowercase p on the card, then the pig and the word Pig. Ask which letter hung its belly low — big P wears its belly up on the stick, little p lets it dangle below.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does P make?" "Can you make my tissue jump?" "What p-words are trotting around this room?" — answered with a name, a clean puff, a gust of air and a happy hunt.

    What your child can say or do

    "Puh! Puh-pig!" Expect tissue-jumping demonstrations for every visitor, p-sounds offered to pets and puddles, and trots around the kitchen at suppertime. Oinks may punctuate conversations indefinitely. Consider it fluency.

    Out in the real world

    P puffs through the day: potty, park, pasta, please, the p of a puddle being jumped. Every tiny gust is the card again — and every real pig met at a farm is the sound effect arriving in person.

    Try it together

    Tissue tester: everyone holds a tissue at lip height, and the challenge is to make it jump with the smallest possible puh — then the biggest. Small puffs, giant puffs, whisper puffs: the sound gets a whole gust range before snack.

    Understanding check

    Ask what P says: a short puff that moves a tissue means the sound landed with its gust intact. A little p traced in the air — stick first, dangling belly second — completes the barnyard.

    Parent tips

    If puffs keep turning into buzzes, it is the P-B twin thing and it is fine: hold your throat and let your child discover which one purrs. The trotting game teaches more than any correction ever will.

    Staying safe

    Trotting needs cleared floor and watchful knees — hands-and-knees pigs must steer around table legs. Tissues stay out of mouths, and the game ends while the giggles are still the friendly kind.

    This lesson pairs with the Pig flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS
