    Queen — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson parades: your child learns that q never appears without u at its side, blends their two sounds into one kwuh, and rules a kitchen kingdom from a paper crown.

    What is this?

    Q is the seventeenth letter of the alphabet. It nearly always arrives with its friend u, and the two together say kwuh — the start of queen, quick and quack. One sound, two letters, a team.

    What does it mean?

    Q is the alphabet’s first famous friendship: q and u holding hands on almost every page. Framing that as a best-friends story turns a spelling fact into something a three-year-old finds charming.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called Q; the sound is kwuh, said by q and u together. Q standing alone is rare and can wait years — on this card the friends travel as a pair and the crown does the rest.

    Why this matters

    A letter with a built-in story and a built-in costume is a gift: crowns get made, parades get held, and kwuh gets rehearsed from the throne. The friendship idea also quietly explains why qu-words never split.

    What it teaches

    Two-letter sound blending (qu said as one), letter recognition in two cases, craft skills with paper and stickers, royal-wave motor planning, and the social idea that some letters work as teams.

    Words to learn

    Qqueenqukwuhcrownwave

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter Q — hello, Q! And look: u comes too, because q and u are best friends. Together they say kwuh — like the start of quick! Try it: kwuh, kwuh, queen! Now crown yourself, wave like royalty, and let the parade begin. Long live the queen!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and tell the friendship first: this is the letter Q, and this is a queen — and wherever q goes, u goes too. They are a team.
    2. Make the team sound: kwuh — q and u said together, like the start of quick. Try kwuh three times, then kwuh-queen.
    3. Trace big Q — a round circle with a small tail at the bottom — and little q: a circle with a tail that dangles low, like a wand.
    4. Make paper crowns: decorate, then tape them on. Everyone wears one; royalty must practise the royal wave before parading.
    5. Hold the parade: march through the kitchen saying kwuh, kwuh, queen! and salute your loyal subjects — the chairs, the teddies, the dog if one agrees.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase Q and the little lowercase q on the card, then the queen and the word Queen. Ask which letter has grown a tail — big Q wears a small one at its bottom, little q lets its tail hang low.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound do q and u make together?" "Which letter is q’s best friend?" "Shall we parade past the chairs again?" — answered with a name, a blended kwuh, a proud u and a royal wave.

    What your child can say or do

    "Kwuh! Kwuh-queen!" Expect crowns worn to breakfast, kwuh-sounds offered to quilts and questions, and parades organised at royal short notice. Q and u may be declared best friends in drawings too. The friendship has been internalised.

    Out in the real world

    Q arrives quietly in daily life: quick, quiet, quack at the duck pond, quilt on the bed. Every kwuh is the team sound — and every picture-book queen is the card waving from the page.

    Try it together

    Royal parade: crowns on, one leader, everyone else as subjects. The parade only advances on kwuh — call the sound, take three royal steps. Change leaders at each chair so the smallest subject also gets to rule.

    Understanding check

    Ask what Q says: a kwuh with both letters mentioned together means the team idea landed. A little q traced in the air — circle, then tail — completes the coronation.

    Parent tips

    Q alone can wait for school years — never quiz it now. If u gets forgotten, draw the two letters holding hands on paper once; the story does the memory work better than repeating the fact.

    Staying safe

    Crown-making means grown-up scissors for cutting and tape instead of staples near small heads. Parades need clear floor and no sprinting in socks, and royal waving stays indoors-safe, away from lamps and shelves.

    This lesson pairs with the Queen flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Rainbow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson rumbles: your child switches on a growl that lasts all breath long, draws a rainbow one rrr per band, and traces a letter with a leg kicking out to the side.

    What is this?

    R is the eighteenth letter of the alphabet. Big R and little r make the r sound — rrr, the growl of a friendly dog, the rumble of a small engine. Start it and hold it: the sound rumbles as long as you like.

    What does it mean?

    R is a holdable sound, which makes it measurable: long rrrs, short rrs, growling contests. Children who struggle to hear tiny sounds often find held ones easier — R is their friend.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called R; the sound is rrr, a growl with the voice on. Some tongues curl for it, some do not, and both are correct — the rumble is what counts, not the tongue’s style.

    Why this matters

    Rainbows are headline news at three, so the word arrives pre-loaded with excitement. Drawing the bands one rrr at a time stretches one word into a whole craft session of sound practice.

    What it teaches

    Sustained-voice sound production, sound-length control, letter recognition in two cases, crayon arc-drawing for pre-writing curves, and colour naming layered onto phonics for a two-in-one lesson.

    Words to learn

    Rrainbowrrrgrowlcoloursarc

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter R — hello, R! R says rrr — a growl, like a friendly dog. Switch your voice on and hold it: rrrrrr. Feel the rumble? Now say it with me: rrr, rrr, rainbow! And let us draw one — a growl for every band. What a colourful letter."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and point up high: this is the letter R, and this is a rainbow — the sky’s most famous arc.
    2. Make the growl: switch your voice on and rumble — rrrrr, like a friendly dog. Hold it long, then clip it short: rrr, rrr, rainbow.
    3. Trace big R — tall line down, small belly at the top, then a leg kicking out — and little r: a short stick with one small shoulder.
    4. Draw a rainbow together: one rrr per colour band, drawn as arcs across the paper. Three bands is a fine rainbow; seven is the deluxe edition.
    5. End with an r-hunt: find three things that start with the growl — a red crayon, a toy rabbit, somebody’s rosy cheek — and rumble the sound at each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase R and the little lowercase r on the card, then the rainbow and the word Rainbow. Ask which letter grew a leg — big R kicks one out from its belly, little r keeps just a shoulder.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does R make?" "How long can you hold your growl?" "Which colour comes next on our rainbow?" — answered with a name, a rumbling rrr, a breath record and a colour choice.

    What your child can say or do

    "Rrr! Rrr-rainbow!" Expect growls at passing dogs and engines, r-sounds offered to running and rabbits, and rainbows requested on every grey day. The growl contest may need a referee. Colouring in becomes sound practice.

    Out in the real world

    R rumbles through the day: rain, run, red, round, room. Every growl is the card rehearsing — and every real rainbow spotted from a window or a car seat becomes the letter’s own celebration parade.

    Try it together

    Growl and draw: move the crayon across the paper only while the growl lasts — rrrrrr keeps the line travelling, silence stops it. One long growl makes one long band. Fill the rainbow together, one held sound per colour.

    Understanding check

    Ask what R says: a growl with the voice switched on and holdable length means the sound landed. A little r traced in the air — stick, then shoulder — completes the arc.

    Parent tips

    Both tongue versions of rrr are correct, so never correct tongue shape — rumble on. If the growl will not start, try an engine sound first; cars have been teaching this letter for decades.

    Staying safe

    Crayons stay on paper — walls grow their own rainbows otherwise, which is a different lesson. Growling contests pause for breath-catchers, and rainbow-spotting from windows and car seats stays seated and supervised.

    This lesson pairs with the Rainbow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Sun — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson stretches: your child hisses a sound that can outlast anyone’s patience, points to the teeth doing the work, becomes a sunbeam on command and traces the curviest letter yet.

    What is this?

    S is the nineteenth letter of the alphabet. Big S and little s make the s sound — sss, a hiss like a snake or a tyre letting air out gently. The teeth do the work; the breath does the rest.

    What does it mean?

    S is the stretchiest sound in the set: long, short, loud or whispery, one letter with an entire orchestra of practice. And sun is a word children meet in books long before breakfast.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called S; the sound is sss — a clean hiss, voice off, teeth nearly together. Stretch it long or clip it short; either way the throat stays quiet, because a buzzing sss is Z sneaking in.

    Why this matters

    A sound with a built-in contest (who runs out of air first?) and a built-in game (freeze as a sunbeam) fills a whole afternoon. The smiling sun on the card does half the welcoming by itself.

    What it teaches

    Long-airflow hiss control, teeth placement awareness, voice-off discrimination, letter recognition in two cases, and whole-body stillness on cue — freeze games train the stopping muscle as much as the starting one.

    Words to learn

    Ssunssshissstretchfreeze

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter S — hello, S! S says sss — a hiss, like a snake in the grass. Teeth together, breath out: sssss. How long can you hold it? Now be a sunbeam — arms out, turn around slowly... sss-sun! Freeze! Lovely and sunny. Then trace the big S: slide down like a snake."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and squint at it: this is the letter S, and this is the sun — smiling, with rays to point at.
    2. Make the hiss: teeth nearly closed, breath sliding out — sssss. Point at your own teeth: they are the players. Try a long sss, then three short ones.
    3. Trace big S — one winding curve from top to bottom, like a snake sliding downhill — and little s: the same wiggle, smaller.
    4. Play sunbeams: stretch your arms out wide, turn slowly while hissing sss-sun, and freeze into a sunny statue the moment you call freeze.
    5. End with an s-hunt: find three things that start with the hiss — a sock, a spoon, a smile — and hiss the sound at each one.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase S and the little lowercase s on the card, then the smiling sun and the word Sun. Ask which letter wiggles more — both Ss wind down the page in curves, one big and one small.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does S make?" "Can your hiss beat mine for length?" "Can you freeze like a sunbeam?" — answered with a name, a clean sss, an epic breath-off and one statue-still sunbeam.

    What your child can say or do

    "Sss! Sss-sun!" Expect hisses at snakes in books, s-sounds offered to socks and sausages, and sunbeam freezing whenever music stops anywhere in the house. The hiss contest may settle sibling disputes. Possibly not peacefully.

    Out in the real world

    S hisses through the day: sun on the curtains, soup at lunch, sleep at bedtime, the slide at the park. Every hiss is the card rehearsing — and every sunny morning is the letter arriving in the window.

    Try it together

    Sss contest: faces close, one long hiss each — first out of air becomes the sun for the next round, arms out wide while everyone hisses at them. Then the sun hisses back. Nobody truly wins; everybody practises.

    Understanding check

    Ask what S says: a long clean hiss with voice off means the sound landed — check the throat stays quiet, because buzzing means z sneaked in. A wiggly little s traced in the air completes the sunshine.

    Parent tips

    S invites exaggeration — let the hisses be enormous at first, then normal-sized. If a buzz appears, that is Z’s sound visiting; keep your own throat silent and let your child find the quiet version by listening.

    Staying safe

    Sunbeam spinning happens in cleared space, slow turns only, with breaks before dizziness wins. Real sunshine needs hats and shade; the hissing can move indoors, where the freezing is safer anyway.

    This lesson pairs with the Sun flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Turtle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson slows down: your child taps a quick tuh behind their teeth, walks the world’s slowest laps of the living room and traces a letter made of two clean lines.

    What is this?

    T is the twentieth letter of the alphabet. Big T and little t make the t sound — tuh, a quick tap of the tongue on the ridge behind the top teeth. Tap once and the word is away.

    What does it mean?

    T is a speed lesson disguised as a slow one: the sound is a single fast tap, but the turtle insists on walking pace. Fast sound, slow feet — the contrast keeps both facts memorable.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called T; the sound is a short clean tap — tuh, tongue on the ridge, no buzzing. Tap it twice — tuh-tuh — and you can feel the letter working. D is its cousin: same spot, voice on.

    Why this matters

    Slow-motion games are comedy gold at three, and the turtle is their patron saint. A letter that arrives with permission to be extremely slow gets practised far longer than a rushed one ever does.

    What it teaches

    Tongue-tap precision, voiced-versus-voiceless discrimination, letter recognition in two cases, balance and slow-motion body control, and the patience to finish a full lap without bursting into a trot.

    Words to learn

    Tturtletuhtapslowsteady

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter T — hello, T! T says tuh — the tongue taps behind the top teeth, quick as this: tuh! Feel the tap? Now be a turtle with me: one slow step... tuh... another slow step... tuh. Slow and steady wins the alphabet. Then trace the big T: tall line, arms out straight."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and admire the pace: this is the letter T, and this is a turtle — the slowest teacher in the alphabet.
    2. Make the tap: tongue taps the ridge behind your top teeth — tuh. Quick! Tap twice: tuh-tuh. Find the spot with one slow tap first.
    3. Trace big T — one tall line down and one straight arm across the top — and little t: a shorter stick with a crossbar and a small curve at its foot.
    4. Walk like turtles: very slow steps around the room, one tuh per step. Slow-motion races are allowed; real hurrying breaks turtle law.
    5. End with a t-hunt: find three things that start with the tap — a toe, a tooth, a teddy — and tap the sound onto each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase T and the little lowercase t on the card, then the turtle and the word Turtle. Ask which letter holds its arms higher — big T spreads a straight line across its very top, little t wears its crossbar lower down.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does T make?" "Where does your tongue tap?" "Can you take one genuinely slow turtle step?" — answered with a name, a crisp tuh, a pointed tongue and a heroic crawl.

    What your child can say or do

    "Tuh! Tuh-turtle!" Expect slow-motion walks everywhere, t-sounds offered to toes and toothbrushes, and turtle law invoked at bedtime. The tap is quick; everything else about this lesson stays slow. That is precisely the charm.

    Out in the real world

    T taps through the day: toast, teeth, time for bed, tickle — some of the busiest words in a toddler’s vocabulary. Every tap is the card again, and a real turtle met at a pond is the lesson walking off at its own pace.

    Try it together

    Turtle race: pick a finish line three metres away and cross it in the slowest steps anyone can manage — first to finish last wins. One tuh per step, wobbling encouraged, trotting disqualifies the whole species.

    Understanding check

    Ask what T says: a quick tongue-tap with no buzz behind it means the sound landed clean. A big-armed T traced in the air — line down, arms across — completes the slow parade.

    Parent tips

    Keep the tap crisp: tuh, not tuuuh — the turtle is slow, the sound is not. If D and T get confused, tap both slowly and let your child feel which one buzzes; the tongue already knows the spot.

    Staying safe

    Turtle racing happens on open floor with room to wobble — bare feet or grippy socks on smooth floors. Slow-motion is not hands-free climbing: shells stay on the ground, and laps end before legs do.

    This lesson pairs with the Turtle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Umbrella — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hops: your child finds the sneakiest vowel sound there is, jumps up on uh and ducks low on under, opens an imaginary umbrella and traces the letter shaped like a cup.

    What is this?

    U is the twenty-first letter of the alphabet. In umbrella, it makes its short sound: uh — like the start of up and under. Say uh-umbrella and shrug your shoulders high on the uh.

    What does it mean?

    U is the hardest vowel to hear at the front of a word, which is exactly why it needs such a friendly prop. The umbrella turns a slippery sound into a thing you can open, hold and duck beneath.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called U; in umbrella it says uh — short and relaxed, the mouth barely doing anything, which is why it hides. If your child offers the letter’s name instead, that is correct information too; the short sound arrives with practice.

    Why this matters

    A vowel that hides needs a body game: springing up on uh and ducking low on under plants the sound in muscle memory. And rainy days become letter days, which is excellent weather planning.

    What it teaches

    Tricky-vowel sound isolation, sound-and-action pairing with vertical movement, letter recognition in two cases, shoulder shrugs and crouching for gross-motor range, and listening for sounds buried inside words.

    Words to learn

    Uumbrellauhupunderrain

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter U — hello, U! In umbrella, U says uh — short and quick, like the start of up. Say it with a shrug: uh! Now play it with me — spring up on uh, duck down low on under, and stretch up big on umbrella! Then trace the big U: down, round the bottom, and up. A cup of a letter."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and unfold the story: this is the letter U, and this is an umbrella — ready for rain, exactly like its sound is ready to hide.
    2. Make the sound: uh — short, relaxed, the sound at the start of up. Try uh three times, shrugging your shoulders up each time.
    3. Trace big U — down, curve along the bottom, up the other side, like a cup — and little u: the same cup, smaller.
    4. Play the up-under game: spring up on uh, duck low on under, spring up again on umbrella. Your body spells the words while your mouth says them.
    5. End with a uh-hunt: find two things whose names hide the uh sound — one thing up high, one thing hiding under the table — and shrug the sound out of each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase U and the little lowercase u on the card, then the umbrella and the word Umbrella. Ask what shape the letters hold — both Us curve like an open cup, ready to catch the rain.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What does U say in umbrella?" "Can you spring up on uh and duck on under?" "What is hiding under the table right now?" — answered with a name, a short uh, one jump, one duck and a discovery.

    What your child can say or do

    "Uh! Uh-umbrella!" Expect shoulder-shrugs mid-word, uh-sounds offered to upside-down things, and umbrella-opening at the first grey cloud. The up-under game may need referee-like fairness. Rain becomes a phonics forecast.

    Out in the real world

    U umbrellas itself through the week: up, under, umbrella at the door, underpants at laundry time. Every shrugging uh is the card rehearsing — and every rainy walk is the letter standing open in your child’s hand.

    Try it together

    Up-under-umbrella: call the words at random — up means a big hop, under means a low duck, umbrella means arms overhead in a dome. Mix the order faster and faster until the giggles win, then finish with one calm cup traced in the air.

    Understanding check

    Ask what U says in umbrella: a short relaxed uh with a shoulder-shrug means the slippery sound landed. A little u traced in the air — one smooth cup — completes the rainy-day kit.

    Parent tips

    If the letter’s name shows up instead of the sound, accept it warmly — both facts are true — then model uh inside up and under and let the short version creep in through the game. Shrugs help; lectures never do.

    Staying safe

    Hopping and ducking need cleared floor and soft landings — no umbrella-arms near lamps or shelves. Real umbrellas open with a grown-up’s help, away from eyes, and stay outdoors where the rain is.

    This lesson pairs with the Umbrella flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Van — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson delivers: your child switches on a throat-buzz with teeth resting on their lip, loads a laundry basket with parcels and drives the whole house one vvv at a time.

    What is this?

    V is the twenty-second letter of the alphabet. Big V and little v make the v sound — vvv, made by setting your top teeth against your bottom lip and letting the voice hum. Hold your throat: the engine is running.

    What does it mean?

    V is F’s twin with the motor switched on: same lips, one purrs and one whispers. Children feel that difference in their throat long before they can explain it, which is the perfect order to learn it in.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called V; the sound is vvv — teeth on lip, voice buzzing, no puff. Hold it as long as breath allows; the van never stops idling. F is the quiet twin, one throat-check away.

    Why this matters

    Vans arrive at real doors most weeks, so the word renews itself in the wild. And a sound with a built-in engine invites a whole driving game — buzzing is the fuel and the phonics at once.

    What it teaches

    Voiced friction sound production, throat-feeling for voice-on versus voice-off, letter recognition in two cases, basket-lugging and route-planning pretend play, and polite door-knocking turn-taking.

    Words to learn

    Vvanvvvbuzzteethparcels

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter V — hello, V! V says vvv — teeth on your lip, and switch your voice on: vvv. Feel your throat buzzing? That is the engine! Now load the van — vvv, vvv, van! — and drive it to the door. Beep beep! Parcel for the teddy, please."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and listen: this is the letter V, and this is a van — hear that engine? It is already saying the sound.
    2. Make the buzz: top teeth rest on your bottom lip and the voice hums — vvv. Hold your throat and feel it running. Try a long vvv, then vvv-van.
    3. Trace big V — two lines sliding down to meet at a point — and little v: the same shape, smaller. Both look like a bird’s beak.
    4. Load the van: parcels into a laundry basket, then drive the route — vvv, vvv, van! — around the house with beeps at the corners.
    5. End with a v-hunt: deliver three parcels to three rooms, one vvv per doorstep, and knock politely — vvv is also for visitor.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase V and the little lowercase v on the card, then the van and the word Van. Ask what shape the letters make — two lines sliding down to meet in one sharp point, like a beak.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does V make?" "Can you feel the engine in your throat?" "Where shall we deliver the next parcel?" — answered with a name, a buzzing vvv, a hand on the throat and a route plan.

    What your child can say or do

    "Vvv! Vvv-van!" Expect engine sounds on every delivery day, v-sounds offered to vegetables and violins, and baskets driven through the house at respectable speeds. Parcels may be wrapped in everything. The buzz has been switched on.

    Out in the real world

    V vrooms through the week: vans at the door, vegetables at dinner, visits to grandma. Every buzzing vvv is the card idling — and every real van spotted at the lights is the lesson driving past, beep beeping.

    Try it together

    Parcel run: wrap two or three toys in tea towels, load the basket-van and deliver each one with a long vvv, a beep beep and a polite knock. Swap driver and customer; the customer answers the door saying vvv.

    Understanding check

    Ask what V says: a buzzing vvv with teeth resting on the lip means the sound landed with its engine running. A little v traced in the air — two lines to a point — completes the delivery round.

    Parent tips

    V and f are the same mouth shape, so compare them at the throat once — the purr is V, the whisper is F — then let the driving game do the rest. Buzz length is free practice: long vvv, short vvv, vvv-van.

    Staying safe

    Driving games keep baskets on the floor and routes free of stairs and cables. Beeping stays at indoor volume, parcels contain nothing breakable or small enough to swallow, and parking happens before teatime.

    This lesson pairs with the Van flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Whale — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson surfaces: your child rounds their lips into a little circle for wuh, crouches small and rises like a whale spouting, and traces the letter that looks like two valleys.

    What is this?

    W is the twenty-third letter of the alphabet. Big W and little w make the w sound — wuh, made by rounding your lips into a small circle, like blowing a kiss and talking at once.

    What does it mean?

    W is the only sound with a lip-shape this round, which makes it visible from across the room: watch for the fish-mouth. The whale spout then gives the sound a whole body to rise through.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called W; the sound is wuh — round lips, quick and smooth. The name looks like double-u, and in several languages it is exactly that; whichever name keeps your child talking about whales is the right one.

    Why this matters

    A rise-from-the-floor game turns the sound into a wave: curl, whooo, spout, splash. And whales are the giants of every animal book, so the card arrives with respect already attached.

    What it teaches

    Round-lip sound production, breath rising with whole-body movement, letter recognition in two cases, crouch-and-rise core strength, and pretend water play that builds ocean vocabulary alongside.

    Words to learn

    Wwhalewuhroundspoutsplash

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter W — hello, W! W says wuh — round your lips into a little circle, then let the sound out: wuh! Kissy-lips with a voice. Now be a whale: curl down small... rise up slow... whooo... and SPLASH, the spout goes up! Then trace the big W: down, up, down, up."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and dive in: this is the letter W, and this is a whale — the biggest animal the alphabet knows.
    2. Make the sound: round your lips into a small circle — wuh, a gentle kiss with a voice behind it. Try wuh three times, then wuh-whale.
    3. Trace big W — down, up, down, up: two valleys side by side — and little w: the same two valleys, smaller.
    4. Play the spout: curl down small like a whale underwater, rise up slowly saying whooo, then throw your arms up as the water sprays — splash!
    5. End with a w-hunt: find three things that start with the round-lip sound — a window, some water, somebody’s wrist — and round your lips at each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase W and the little lowercase w on the card, then the whale and the word Whale. Ask what shape the letters make — two dips like waves, one after the other, rolling across the card.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does W make?" "Can you show me the round lips?" "How big was your whale spout this time?" — answered with a name, a round wuh, a fish-mouth and two arms full of imaginary water.

    What your child can say or do

    "Wuh! Wuh-whale!" Expect kissy-lips at bath time, w-sounds offered to water and windows, and spout-jumping wherever floor space allows. Rising whales may appear from every crouch. Bath time becomes the best classroom in the house.

    Out in the real world

    W washes through the day: water, window, wellington boots, weekend. Every round-lipped wuh is the card surfacing — and every whale in a picture book is the spout game waiting for its next performance.

    Try it together

    Whale rise: crouch on the floor, rise on a long whooo and sink back down with a splash — five rises is a full whale morning. Add a shallow bowl of real water for fingertip dips only, one drop per spout.

    Understanding check

    Ask what W says: a smooth round-lip wuh means the sound landed — watch for the fish-mouth to be sure. A wiggly little w traced in the air, two valleys deep, completes the ocean.

    Parent tips

    If the lips stay flat, model the kissy-circle in a mirror without saying anything — the shape teaches itself. Double-u or wuh: let your child use whichever name keeps them talking about whales.

    Staying safe

    Whale rises need headroom and clear floor — spouting arms steer around lamps and siblings. Real water play stays a shallow fingertip splash with a towel ready, and crouching whales surface before their legs fall asleep.

    This lesson pairs with the Whale flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Xylophone — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson crosses over: your child meets the letter that lives at the ends of words, walks a taped X like a tightrope, hunts for things that finish with x and keeps one mystery.

    What is this?

    X is the twenty-fourth letter of the alphabet. Its honest job is ending words — box, fox, six — where it says a ksss sound at the finish. Xylophone is the most famous X word of all, and the reason is funny: x hardly ever starts words, so this card borrows a word that actually begins with a z sound.

    What does it mean?

    X is the one card that teaches a limitation openly, and children find the honesty delightful: x has a job, it mostly works at the ends, and xylophone is the alphabet’s own magic trick.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called X — said as ex. Its sound is the ksss tail at the end of words like box and fox. Xylophone starts with a z sound, and that mystery needs no solving today; the name and the shape are the whole lesson.

    Why this matters

    X arrives with crossing shapes built in: arms crossed, tape crossed, mallets tapped together. And the end-of-word hunt gives x a game no other letter can copy — x is the finisher.

    What it teaches

    End-of-word sound listening (a skill no earlier card has asked for), crossed-lines visual tracking, letter recognition in two cases, balance-beam walking on tape, and pride in saying the name ex clearly.

    Words to learn

    Xxylophoneexboxfoxends

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter X — say its name with me: ex! X is the letter that finishes words: box... fox... Did you hear the ksss at the end? Now walk the crossing tape, arms out like a tightrope walker. And the xylophone? Its first sound is a z — a mystery we keep for another day. Ex-cellent."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and introduce the mystery politely: this is the letter X — said ex — and this is a xylophone, the word where a z quietly sits in for x at the front.
    2. Make the honest sound at word-ends: box, fox — hear the ksss tail? Say box, fox, six, clipping the x neatly at each finish.
    3. Trace big X — two lines crossing, like arms folded — and little x: the same cross, smaller. Draw both in the air, then on the floor with tape.
    4. Walk the tape-X like a tightrope: one foot after the other along one strip, then cross to the other. Two crossings is a full concert.
    5. End with an end-of-word hunt: find something that finishes with x — a box lid, a fox picture, a shoebox — and tap it while saying the whole word slowly.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase X and the little lowercase x on the card, then the xylophone and the word Xylophone. Ask what shape the letters make — two lines crossed in the middle, like a pair of crossed mallets.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does x make at the end of box?" "Can you walk the crossing tape without wobbling off?" "What else ends with x?" — answered with ex, a clipped ksss, two crossings and a hunted box.

    What your child can say or do

    "Ex! Box ends with x!" Expect x-clipping at the end of every box and fox mentioned, tightrope walks across taped floors, and drum solos on anything mallet-shaped. The z-mystery may be revealed to strangers. Keep it mysterious a little longer.

    Out in the real world

    X crosses paths at the ends: a box of tissues, foxes in storybooks, six biscuits, the x on a treasure map. Every clipped ksss is the card finishing its word — and X-marks-the-spot drawings put the letter to work at once.

    Try it together

    X marks the spot: draw a treasure map with a big X, hide a small treasure somewhere in the room and let your child follow clues to the crossing point. Each clue brings them ex-citingly closer until the treasure is found on the X.

    Understanding check

    Ask what X is called — ex — and what it does at the end of box: a clear ex and a clipped ksss mean both facts landed. A big crossing X traced in the air completes the concert.

    Parent tips

    The z-sound at the start of xylophone is a known mystery — park it cheerfully rather than explaining phonics history at three. Practise the end-of-word ksss more than the name; the ending is x’s real job and the best preparation.

    Staying safe

    Tape the X flat with no curled edges to trip on, and keep tightrope walking on non-slip floors in bare feet. Toy mallets stay for the xylophone only — drumming happens on boxes and keys, never on siblings or screens.

    This lesson pairs with the Xylophone flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Yo-yo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson bounces: your child makes the yuh sound with a hand-bounce for every letter, becomes the yo-yo in a sink-and-spring game, and traces the letter that plants one leg on the ground.

    What is this?

    Y is the twenty-fifth letter of the alphabet. In yo-yo, it makes its friendly starting sound: yuh — like the start of yes and yarn. Say yuh-yo-yo with a little hand-bounce on every yuh.

    What does it mean?

    Y is a two-job letter — it sometimes works as a vowel — but this card does not mention any of that. Here y is pure toy box: down it goes, up it comes, and the sound rides along both ways.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called Y; in yo-yo it says yuh, a quick friendly sound at the front of the mouth. The middle-of-word y in happy and funny borrows another sound entirely — next year’s story, not today’s.

    Why this matters

    A toy every relative owns makes the word instantly familiar, and be-the-yo-yo turns the sound into the game: yuh down, yuh up. The repetition is built into the toy’s whole personality.

    What it teaches

    Front-of-mouth glide production, sound-and-action synchrony on vertical movement, letter recognition in two cases, squat-and-stand core strength, and the gentle comedy of being a toy on a string.

    Words to learn

    Yyo-yoyuhdownupspring

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter Y — hello, Y! Y says yuh, like the start of yes. Say it with a bounce: yuh-yo-yo! Now be the yo-yo: stand tall... sink all the way down... and spring back up! Yuh! Again! You are the bounciest letter in the alphabet. Then trace the big Y — arms first, then one leg down."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and wind up: this is the letter Y, and this is a yo-yo — down it goes, up it comes, all day long.
    2. Make the sound: yuh, like the start of yes. Say yuh-yo-yo and give a hand-bounce on every yuh — down, up, down, up.
    3. Trace big Y — two arms meeting in the middle, then one leg straight down to the line — and little y: an arm, a slide and a tail that dips below.
    4. Now be the yo-yo yourself: stand tall, sink all the way down slowly, then spring back up — yuh-yo-yo! Three slow bounces is a complete performance.
    5. End with a yuh-hunt: find three things whose names start with the sound — a toy yak, yesterday’s drawing, a yawn you can demonstrate — and hand-bounce the sound at each.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase Y and the little lowercase y on the card, then the yo-yo and the word Yo-yo. Ask which letter reaches the ground — big Y plants one leg on the line, little y lets its tail dangle below it.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What does Y say in yo-yo?" "Can you sink down slowly and spring back up?" "Can you do a pretend yawn for me?" — answered with a name, a bounced yuh, one full sink-and-spring and a yawn on demand.

    What your child can say or do

    "Yuh! Yuh-yo-yo!" Expect sink-and-spring games in every open patch of floor, y-sounds offered to yoghurt and yawns, and hand-bounces added to ordinary sentences. Being a toy is a career now. The alphabet provided.

    Out in the real world

    Y yo-yos through the week: yes at full volume, yoghurt at breakfast, the yard, the yellow crayon. Every yuh is the card bouncing — and any real yo-yo found in a drawer is the lesson on a string, ready to perform.

    Try it together

    Be the yo-yo: a grown-up holds an invisible string and calls the speed — slow sink, fast spring, wobbly middle — while your child plays the toy. Then swap: you be the yo-yo and let your child run the string. Being the caller is the better half.

    Understanding check

    Ask what Y says in yo-yo: a quick friendly yuh with a hand-bounce means the sound landed. A little y traced in the air — arm, slide, dangling tail — completes the toy box.

    Parent tips

    Keep y’s vowel career entirely off the agenda — happy and funny can wait years. If the sink becomes a drop, slow it right down; the spring is the reward, and slow sinks make better springs.

    Staying safe

    Yo-yo sinking happens on clear floor with soft landings — no sinking near table corners, and hands stay free to catch balance. Real yo-yos are for older hands at this age; the body version is safer and funnier anyway.

    This lesson pairs with the Yo-yo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Zebra — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson finishes in style: your child switches the buzz onto the s sound, draws stripes while zzz-ing, traces the last letter of the alphabet and celebrates twenty-six doors opened.

    What is this?

    Z is the twenty-sixth and last letter of the alphabet. It makes the z sound — zzz, the same hiss as s with the voice switched on. Hold your throat and compare: s whispers, z hums like a tiny bee.

    What does it mean?

    Z closes the set with a sound your child already owns: they have been hissing sss since the sun card, and z is that hiss with the motor on. Ending by upgrading a known sound is the gentlest finale there is.

    What does the child need to know?

    The letter is called Z; the sound is zzz — voice on, teeth close, a buzz you can hold. Z is also the sideways letter: tip a z onto its back and you have drawn a stripe, which the zebra demonstrates gladly.

    Why this matters

    Finishing the alphabet deserves a fanfare, and stripes give small fingers a road to trace from the letter to the animal and back again. The celebration is real: your child now owns a door for every sound.

    What it teaches

    Voiced sibilant production (s with the voice switched on), letter recognition across the whole set, stripe-line drawing for controlled strokes, and the happy memory work of recalling favourite letters from A to Z.

    Words to learn

    Zzebrazzzbuzzstripesfinish

    Say this to your child

    “"This is the letter Z — hello, Z! The very last letter! Z says zzz — start with a hiss, sss, then switch your voice on: zzz. Feel it buzz like a tiny bee? Now draw stripes with me — zzz, zzz, zebra! And then... the whole alphabet, from A all the way here. You did it. Twenty-six letters, all yours."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and announce the finale: this is the letter Z — the very last one — and this is a zebra, dressed for the occasion.
    2. Make the buzz: hiss sss first, then switch your voice on — zzz. Feel your throat purr? Try sss-zzz, sss-zzz, and hear the twins.
    3. Trace big Z — straight across, slide down, straight across, like a zigzag — and little z: the same zigzag, smaller.
    4. Draw stripes: across a paper zebra, or up your own arm with a washable marker — one zzz per stripe. Stripes are only the letter z tipped on its side.
    5. End with the grand tour: say the alphabet together, naming every letter you both met this year, and give Z three final zzz-buzzes for the road.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the big uppercase Z and the little lowercase z on the card, then the zebra and the word Zebra. Ask what the letters and the animal share — stripes run across the page the same way a z lies sideways.

    Ask your child

    "What is this letter called?" "What sound does Z make?" "How is zzz different from sss?" "Can you name your favourite letter of all?" — answered with a name, a buzzing zzz, a throat-check answer and a proud choice.

    What your child can say or do

    "Zzz! Zzz-zebra!" Expect buzzes at sleeping cats and bees, z-sounds offered to zips and zooms, and stripes counted on every zebra in every book. The alphabet tour will be requested nightly. Twenty-six doors, all opening.

    Out in the real world

    Z buzzes softly through the week: zips on coats, zoom through the park, the z of sleeping sounds at naptime. Every buzz is the card celebrating — and the alphabet itself is now a road your child can walk end to end.

    Try it together

    Alphabet tour: lay out as many letter cards as you own — or write letters on paper plates — and walk the whole A-to-Z road together, saying each name and sound at every stop. Z’s stop comes last, with three buzzes and a bow.

    Understanding check

    Ask what Z says: a held buzz with the voice switched on means the sound landed — an sss without buzz is still s. A zigzag little z traced in the air closes the alphabet for good.

    Parent tips

    This is the finish, so let it feel like one: revisit favourite letters, keep the zebra drawing and stop before anyone is tired. The next lessons will find these same letters waiting inside real words — the doors are built; walking them comes next.

    Staying safe

    Washable markers only for arm-stripes, with a patch check on the skin first and no drawing near eyes or mouths. The alphabet tour needs clear walking space, and the celebration ends with tidying up — even zebras help put the cushions back.

    This lesson pairs with the Zebra flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).
